780.bp: Websites need to predict changes in user traffic and behavior patterns before they happen. When usage drops or spikes unpredictably, services crash or waste resources. Time series forecasting (predicting future values in a sequence of numbers, like daily visits) sits at the heart of keeping web services running smoothly.
780.wh: Large language models, which are trained on words and text, struggle with numerical time series because their training data looks nothing like sequences of numbers. Just feeding a time series directly to a frozen language model produces poor predictions. Meanwhile, fine-tuning the model (adjusting its internal weights) is expensive and slow, burning through compute resources.

The core problem: models trained on language understand words, not numbers. Fine-tuning them costs too much compute. But retraining from scratch also fails because the model's learned skills don't transfer to a totally different domain.
780.ap: They inject example numbers into the frozen language model using a learnable adapter—a small neural component that compresses several past examples into a single context vector, then feeds that vector into every layer of the language model during prediction. This vector acts like a translator, telling the frozen model 'here's what recent data looks like' without changing the model's weights.
780.ww: Language models excel at using patterns shown in-context (learning from examples you show them during inference, not retraining). By distilling example time series into a compact vector and injecting it throughout the model, the method hijacks this existing skill—the model learns to interpret the injected numbers as context and adapts its predictions accordingly, all without any retraining.
780.po: The approach keeps the language model frozen (no expensive fine-tuning) while improving forecast accuracy over naive application of the model. This cuts compute overhead drastically while delivering better predictions than a language model used straight out of the box.

781.bp: Creating convincing synthetic speech (voice cloning) is increasingly practical, but doing it via cloud services means your voice recordings—biometric data tied uniquely to you—get sent to a third party and stored somewhere. A person building a speech system needs the capability locally where data never leaves their device.
781.wh: Existing commercial voice cloning services work well but require uploading your voice to their servers, raising privacy and security risks. Building a local system that matches professional quality demands careful engineering: it needs to learn a voice from only a few seconds of audio, adapt to new writing styles with moderate data, and run on regular consumer laptops without special hardware.
781.ap: They package an existing open-source speech architecture (Coqui XTTS-v2) into a locally-run application that can clone a voice from a short 5-10 second sample instantly, or train a custom model from 10-30 minutes of personal audio using a parameter-efficient technique (LoRA—a trick to fine-tune only a tiny fraction of the model's weights). They add data cleaning, verification, and a web interface around it.
781.ww: Running inference locally avoids transmission entirely, eliminating the privacy risk. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) lets the model adapt to a user's voice without retraining everything, keeping latency and memory low. Automating preprocessing and using cosine similarity scores (a mathematical measure of voice match) ensures quality stays high even on consumer hardware.
781.po: Users get professional-quality voice synthesis (similarity score >0.998 on tested hardware) running on their own laptop, never touching a cloud server. The system handles both instant cloning and rapid custom training, with a simple web interface—making privacy-preserving speech synthesis practical for real people.

782.bp: Fake news spreads quickly online and undermines trust in institutions and each other. To combat misinformation at scale, we need automated systems that can verify whether a claim is real or fabricated by finding evidence that corroborates or contradicts it.
782.wh: Simply retrieving documents using the original news headline usually fails because the phrasing of the news doesn't match the phrasing of evidence that would prove or disprove it. A headline might say 'Stock market up' but relevant evidence uses terms like 'equities surge'—lexical mismatch breaks naive search. Meanwhile, existing approaches either tweak the evidence retriever or tweak the fact-checker, leaving the query gap untouched.
782.ap: They train a small language model to act as a query rewriter, taking the original news text and rewriting it into better search queries that will retrieve the most relevant evidence. A frozen large language model then reads the news and the retrieved evidence and makes a verdict. The system iterates: the rewritten queries are refined again based on what was already retrieved, progressively improving the search results fed to the fact-checker.
782.ww: The gap between news phrasing and evidence phrasing is the real bottleneck—a well-formulated search query (written in the language of evidence databases) retrieves far more useful material than the raw headline. By focusing learning on query quality, the system attacks the true problem. Iteration refines queries further, catching evidence the first pass missed.
782.po: The approach consistently improves fake news detection on two real-world datasets. By rewriting and refining search queries, it retrieves more relevant evidence, which feeds a more accurate fact-checking decision—without retraining the frozen fact-checker itself.

783.bp: In networks (social, financial, transportation), some nodes matter more than others—centrality measures quantify importance. Security analysts and investigators rely on these metrics to spot key players and hidden structures. But what if the people you're studying know you're measuring them and want to hide?
783.wh: An adversary can create many fake accounts (Sybil attack) and carefully distribute connections among them to camouflage their true importance. For simple measures like node degree (how many connections), computing the optimal hiding strategy is tractable. But for more sophisticated measures like closeness or betweenness (how much you lie on shortest paths between others), the optimization problem becomes computationally intractable—there's no known efficient algorithm.
783.ap: For the hard cases (closeness, betweenness), they borrow ideas from community detection literature to design practical heuristics—algorithms that don't guarantee optimal answers but work well in practice. These heuristics group and redistribute connections in ways that minimize the attacker's detectability, running in reasonable time on real networks.
783.ww: Real networks have structure (they cluster, have bottlenecks, etc.) that limits how effectively you can hide by adding fake nodes. Community detection algorithms exploit this structure to design hiding strategies that are nearly optimal even though finding the true optimum is mathematically hard. In practice, the constraints of realistic networks make heuristics very effective.
783.po: Experiments on real covert networks show Sybil-based obfuscation substantially outperforms previous hiding techniques. The work highlights a critical vulnerability: security analysts who trust centrality-based identification without accounting for Sybil attacks can be seriously misled, especially on betweenness and closeness metrics.

784.bp: Web services generate massive logs of every transaction and error. When something breaks, engineers dig through logs to find the problem. Automating anomaly detection (finding unusual log entries) saves time and catches issues before they become critical failures.
784.wh: Existing deep learning approaches discard important exact text during preprocessing, making results uninterpretable to engineers ('where did this anomaly come from?'). Other systems use dense numerical representations that hide the original data. Meanwhile, real industrial systems need fast inference on commodity hardware and explainable outputs—you can't explain 'the embedding said so.'
784.ap: They use a language model purely to propose candidate patterns (sequences that look like anomalies), then feed those proposals to a deterministic verifier that confirms or rejects them using mathematical rules. Anomalous patterns are extracted into regular expressions for fast matching. The system refines by creating specialized child patterns and adding targeted exclusions to improve precision.
784.ww: Language models excel at spotting irregular patterns in text without being explicitly programmed. A deterministic verifier (a set of concrete rules) ensures explainability and correctness—engineers can read the regex and understand exactly what the system flagged. Two-stage refinement (increasing recall, then precision) extracts the maximum useful signal from both the model and the rules.
784.po: On three real Huawei Cloud datasets, the system achieves F1 score 0.9877 (very high accuracy), outperforming neural baselines. Logs stay human-readable throughout, regular expressions enable fast online matching on CPUs, and engineers can understand and audit every decision.

785.bp: Short video platforms (TikTok, Instagram Reels) evolve rapidly—new types of harmful content emerge daily (new slang, meme formats, trends). Moderation teams need to spot these emerging issues and update their policies before the content spreads to millions.
785.wh: Human review of emerging issues is slow and reactive. By the time one person flags 'this new trend is problematic,' the video has circulated widely. Traditional rule-based moderation policies miss what they weren't written to catch. Expanding manual review doesn't scale.
785.ap: They deploy a multimodal language model agent (one that understands both images and text) to automatically search for videos with potential unreported issues, cluster similar problematic videos together, and automatically generate updated annotation policies describing the new issue and how to spot it.
785.ww: Language models can reason about visual and textual content at scale, spotting patterns humans would miss. Clustering groups related cases, revealing what the issue actually is. Automatic policy generation turns these discovered issues into actionable rules. The speed—checking thousands of videos in minutes—outpaces any human review process.
785.po: Deployed in a real system, the agent improves emerging-issue discovery (F1 score improvement >20%) and governance (reducing problematic video views by ~15%). More importantly, it dramatically cuts the time needed to detect and respond to trends, allowing policies to stay current rather than perpetually behind.

786.bp: Web designers and 3D artists need to generate realistic materials (wood, metal, plastic surfaces) that look convincing and respond correctly to light in interactive environments. Hand-authoring these textures is slow; automation could accelerate creative workflows.
786.wh: Text descriptions of appearance are ambiguous and incomplete—'shiny silver' could mean many things. RGB texture images (the usual output) bake in shadows and highlights from a single lighting direction, so they look wrong when the light changes. Relying on only one type of guidance limits control.
786.ap: They build a system that takes three kinds of input simultaneously: a reference image (showing fine visual details words can't capture), a text description (conveying the overall intent), and geometric shape information (anchoring the texture to the object's form). The system outputs not RGB pixels but industry-standard material parameters: albedo (base color), metallic (how reflective), and roughness (how smooth or scratched)—separate numbers that work correctly under any lighting.
786.ww: Each input type captures something the others don't: images give high-frequency details, text gives intent, geometry grounds the result spatially. Decoupling into PBR parameters (physical-based rendering) means the material stays realistic under any illumination, essential for dynamic web environments where lighting changes. Multimodal guidance reduces ambiguity.
786.po: The framework produces materials that are both visually high-fidelity and physically consistent, working correctly in web environments with dynamic lighting. Users get better control by combining multiple input types, and artists don't need to hand-tweak materials for different lighting scenarios.

787.bp: Banks and payment networks flag fraud by watching transaction patterns in real time. As new fraud tactics emerge, the detection system must adapt to them. But adapting to new patterns risks 'forgetting' old ones—the system starts missing the fraud tactics it learned previously.
787.wh: As streaming fraud data arrives, models learn new patterns but forget old ones (catastrophic forgetting). Storing historical data to replay and re-learn from it eventually hits storage limits in production systems. Simply ignoring old patterns means old fraud tactics go undetected again.
787.ap: They use a generative model (a system that can create synthetic data) to make fake past transaction examples that preserve the essential characteristics of previously learned fraud patterns, without storing real historical data. The synthetic transactions are created using a diffusion model (a technique that gradually shapes random noise into realistic examples) guided by a hierarchical transformer network that understands the structure of transaction graphs.
787.ww: Synthetic replay preserves learned patterns in a compressed form—the generative model acts like a lossy memory. Diffusion models are good at capturing complex structures (the hierarchy of users, transactions, timestamps). By retraining on synthetic replays alongside new data, the system avoids forgetting while staying within storage budgets.
787.po: On four streaming fraud datasets, the method avoids catastrophic forgetting—the system detects both old and new fraud patterns reliably. Storage requirements stay constant (no accumulating historical data), making it practical for real fraud detection systems at scale.

788.bp: Online memes often carry cultural meanings that vary by region. A meme considered funny in one culture can be hateful in another, or mean something entirely different. Automated content moderation systems need to detect hateful memes across cultures, not just flag what Western training data labels as hateful.
788.wh: Current vision-language models (systems trained to understand images and text together) are trained mostly on Western data and English. They learn what Western moderators found harmful, not what violates norms in other cultures. Translating meme text into English before checking often breaks the meaning—slang and cultural references don't translate cleanly. Zero-shot systems (ones that don't see examples first) perform even worse on unfamiliar content.
788.ap: They evaluate state-of-the-art vision models on culturally diverse meme datasets, testing three variables: whether the model sees examples first (one-shot learning) vs. none (zero-shot), whether prompts are in the original language vs. English, and what happens when meme text is translated. They measure which combinations best detect hateful content across cultures.
788.ww: One-shot learning (showing one example first) gives models context about how this culture uses memes. Native-language prompts don't lose meaning in translation. Together, these strategies align the model's expectations with the target culture, partly overriding Western-centric training. Translation degrades performance because meaning is lost.
788.po: Results show that culturally aligned interventions (native language + one-shot learning) substantially improve hateful meme detection. The work reveals systematic bias toward Western norms and provides concrete strategies (native prompting, example-based learning) to build moderation systems that work fairly across cultures.

789.bp: Understanding emotion in conversations requires reading between the lines—the same words can express different emotions depending on tone of voice and facial expression. Automated emotion recognition from videos (combining text, audio, and video) enables applications from mental health screening to customer service.
789.wh: Video, audio, and text don't always agree or contribute equally. Background noise can make audio useless; poor camera angles can hide facial cues. Simply averaging all three signals lets bad signals drag down performance. Additionally, emotions flow over a conversation—sadness in one turn influences the next, but most systems treat each turn as independent.
789.ap: They build a system that learns which pairs of modalities (audio-video, text-audio, etc.) are high-quality for each utterance, dynamically selecting the best pair for fusion. It uses information theory (mutual information—a mathematical measure of how much two signals tell each other) to decide which modalities align well. A separate neural network (a GRU, a type of recurrent network) tracks emotion changes across the conversation, predicting how emotion evolves turn by turn.
789.ww: Selective fusion based on mutual information keeps noisy modalities from degrading results—it's like letting only the 'confident' signals vote. Tracking emotional trajectory captures real conversational dynamics (anger escalates, sadness lingers), not treating each utterance as a random event. Joint training on both static emotion and dynamic transitions teaches the system to understand both.
789.po: On two benchmark datasets (IEMOCAP and MELD), the approach outperforms existing methods. It correctly identifies emotions more often by tuning fusion to each moment's data quality and by modeling emotion as a flow rather than isolated snapshots.

790.bp: Users on Netflix or Spotify receive recommendations from one platform, but their behavior on other platforms (watching YouTube, reading news sites) hints at preferences that could improve recommendations everywhere. Cross-domain recommendation aims to share signals across platforms—but platforms are separate, so data sharing raises privacy and trust concerns.
790.wh: Federated learning (training without centralizing data) protects privacy but creates new problems: user behavior sequences look different on each platform (what 'binge-watching' means on Netflix vs. YouTube differs). Platforms can't share raw data because of privacy rules. Meanwhile, participants might cheat—servers could lie about performance, clients could send fake updates or collude to poison the shared model.
790.ap: They build a system where each platform learns separately, then shares only learned representations (not raw data). A variational encoder at each platform disentangles what's unique to that platform (domain-exclusive features) from what transfers to others (domain-shared features), enabling privacy-preserving knowledge transfer. A contribution evaluation module tracks which clients and features actually helped—allowing the system to detect when someone is cheating or making things worse.
790.ww: Disentangling domain-shared from domain-exclusive patterns means each platform can skip irrelevant platform-specific quirks and focus on universal preferences—movies watched implies reading preferences. Contribution evaluation prevents negative transfer (bad data poisoning the model) and detects dishonest participants by quantifying each platform's actual value. Together, these enable trustworthy collaboration.
790.po: On real multi-domain datasets, the approach delivers recommendation quality competitive with or better than federated baselines, while maintaining privacy and enabling detection of misbehaving participants. This makes cross-platform recommendation practical in a world where platforms don't fully trust each other.

791.bp: Social media shapes public opinion. Some voices matter more than others in driving what everyone eventually believes. If opinion-formation dynamics are biased (some groups have outsized influence despite equal numbers), that's unfair. Researchers need tools to quantify and correct such imbalance.
791.wh: In the Friedkin-Johnsen model (a math framework for how opinions spread), each person's final opinion is a blend of their inner conviction and peer pressure. 'Stubbornness' controls the blend. The challenge: computing influence (how much each person's inner opinion matters to the crowd) and then adjusting stubbornness to make influence fair across groups, without destabilizing the whole system.
791.ap: They derive mathematical formulas that show exactly how a single person's stubbornness affects everyone's final opinions and influence. Using these formulas, they design efficient algorithms that adjust a few people's stubbornness values to equalize influence across groups. The tweaks are minimal—touching as few people as possible.
791.ww: Closed-form math formulas make the problem tractable: instead of simulating millions of scenarios, algorithms can compute the exact impact of each adjustment. Targeting stubbornness (how anchored you are to your own views) is clever because it naturally models influence—more stubborn people swing opinion more. Minimal interventions preserve the system's stability.
791.po: On both synthetic and real social networks, the algorithms efficiently rebalance influence across groups. The work opens opinion fairness as a research direction and provides concrete methods to reduce bias in how social networks amplify voices.

792.bp: Satellite internet (Starlink, Kuiper) beams data from orbit, extending connectivity to remote areas and disaster zones. But space radiation damages hardware and drains batteries, threatening service continuity. Web services running over these links need to stay online despite radiation.
792.wh: Standard fixes (moving satellites to safer orbits, heating damaged components) consume precious battery power. Other approaches (putting satellites to sleep) cut radiation exposure but interrupt active sessions abruptly. Energy-aware mitigation is missing—the challenge is rerouting traffic intelligently during radiation storms while keeping batteries healthy long-term.
792.ap: They propose RALT, a software layer that monitors space weather and radiation data, then automatically reroutes traffic away from radiation-damaged satellites during storms. The rerouting accounts for remaining battery capacity—moving traffic only to satellites with enough power to handle it, avoiding deep discharge that causes permanent battery aging.
792.ww: Dynamic rerouting keeps traffic flowing without manual intervention. Energy-aware routing prevents the trap where fixing one problem (radiation damage) creates another (battery death). By modeling radiation risk and battery constraints together, the system sustains service instead of trading off resilience against energy efficiency.
792.po: The approach enables reliable web services over LEO satellites despite space radiation. By rethinking resilience through the lens of both radiation and energy, it unlocks satellite internet's potential for global emergency connectivity without sacrificing long-term hardware durability.

793.bp: Recommendation systems often favor certain demographics or items. To be fair, you might want to ensure all groups see diverse recommendations or that less-popular creators get some visibility. But fairness requirements change: one day you prioritize coverage for minority creators, another day you focus on gender balance. Retraining the whole system for each new requirement is prohibitive.
793.wh: Traditional approaches bake fairness into training—once trained for 'maximize coverage for small creators,' the model is locked to that setting. New fairness goals mean starting training from scratch, wasting computation. The tension: how to handle multiple fairness levels without multiple training runs?
793.ap: They build a model that trains once, producing a shared representation of users. On top of that, small adapter modules (like adjustable dials) specialize the representation for different fairness levels. Each level gets its own adapter; the model learns to produce progressively fairer recommendations as the fairness dial turns up. A regularization term ensures improvements don't jump around—they're monotonic (always getting better or staying flat).
793.ww: A shared base representation captures general user preferences. Adapter modules customize that base for different fairness targets, keeping computation lightweight. Monotonic fairness (improvement guaranteed as you turn up the dial) gives users predictable control—increasing fairness never suddenly breaks accuracy.
793.po: Experiments show the framework delivers fairness-accuracy tradeoffs comparable to or better than baselines trained separately for each fairness level—all from a single training run. Users can adjust fairness dynamically without retraining, making fair recommendation practical for platforms with shifting values.

794.bp: Vaccine misinformation (false claims about safety, efficacy, origins) spreads widely in visual formats—memes, infographics, social media posts. Detecting and removing this content at scale is critical for public health, but visual misinformation is harder to analyze automatically than text-only claims.
794.wh: Misinformation in images combines visual elements, text, and cultural/rhetorical cues in complex ways. Direct classification ('is this pro-vaccine or anti-vaccine?') by vision-language models is less accurate than interpretable prediction. Black-box models offer no way for moderators to understand *why* something was flagged, making correction and auditing impossible.
794.ap: They compare two approaches: feeding images directly to a large vision-language model for classification, vs. having the model first extract interpretable concept features (binary True/False flags for specific visual cues like 'contains medical imagery,' 'makes a specific claim'), then training classical machine learning classifiers on these concepts. The second path explains each decision via the concepts that drove it.
794.ww: Concept-grounded prediction is interpretable because concepts (specific visual/textual cues) map to human understanding. A moderator can read 'detected: syringe imagery + false efficacy claim' and immediately understand the signal. Classical ML on concepts is also more accurate—explicit structure guides learning better than dense, opaque model features.
794.po: The concept-grounded approach improves accuracy by 10-17% over direct LVLM classification, while making decisions transparent. Moderators can inspect which visual/rhetorical cues the system noticed, enabling audits and corrections. This hybrid neuro-symbolic approach makes vaccine misinformation detection both more accurate and more trustworthy.
